faq.q: How does light knock electrons free in a solar cell?
faq.a: Each photon of light carries a small packet of energy. When silicon absorbs one, it can give an electron enough energy to break free from its atom and move around.
asks: What does light do to the silicon?

faq.q: Why does a solar cell need two layers?
faq.a: The two layers of treated silicon meet at a junction with a built-in electric field. It pushes freed electrons one way, so they flow as a current instead of just falling back.
asks: What is the p-n junction in a solar cell?

faq.q: How does electricity get out of a solar cell?
faq.a: Thin metal lines on the front and a metal layer on the back collect the electrons. Joined by a wire, they flow round a circuit and back into the cell.
asks: What are the silver lines on a solar cell?

faq.q: What voltage does one solar cell make?
faq.a: A single silicon cell gives about half a volt. A panel joins around 60 cells in series to give a useful voltage, and many panels together can power a house.
asks: Why do solar panels have so many cells?

faq.q: Why are solar cells only about 20 percent efficient?
faq.a: Some light has too little energy to free an electron, and photons with extra energy waste the excess as heat. Some light is also reflected, so typical panels turn about a fifth of the sunlight into electricity.
asks: Where does the rest of the sunlight go?

facts: One silicon solar cell gives about 0.5 to 0.6 volts.
Typical rooftop solar panels convert around 18 to 22 percent of sunlight into electricity.
